meta.blurb: Ten turning points, from a legend about twins and a wolf to the day the last western emperor was sent away. Walk through a thousand years of Rome, five steps at a time, and see why this one city still matters.
meta.bible: A single narrator tells the story of Rome through ten moments, five beats each: 1 the founding legend (about 753 BCE), 2 the end of the kings (509 BCE), 3 the Gauls sack Rome (about 390 BCE), 4 Hannibal and Cannae (216 BCE), 5 Spartacus (73 to 71 BCE), 6 Caesar and the Rubicon (49 BCE) and the Ides of March (44 BCE), 7 Augustus, the first emperor (27 BCE), 8 Vesuvius and Pompeii (79 CE), 9 citizenship for all free people (212 CE), 10 the last western emperor (476 CE). Places: Rome, Tiber, Palatine Hill, Capitoline Hill, Italy, Gaul, Alps, Allia, Carthage, Cannae, Zama, Capua, Vesuvius, Pompeii, Herculaneum, Naples, Bay of Naples, Misenum, Stabiae, Rubicon, Actium, Egypt, Spain, Syria, Britain, Danube, Constantinople, Bosporus, Ravenna, Mediterranean, Thrace, Balkans, Persian Gulf. People (all long dead): Romulus and Remus (legend), Rhea Silvia, Amulius, Faustulus, Tarquin the Proud (last king), Lucretia (legend), Lucius Junius Brutus, Brennus (Gaulish chieftain), Camillus, Marcus Manlius, Hannibal (Carthaginian general), Fabius (the Delayer), Scipio, Spartacus, Marcus Licinius Crassus, Julius Caesar, Pompey, Marcus Brutus, Gaius Cassius, Octavian who became Augustus (died 14 CE), Mark Antony, Cleopatra, Agrippa, Pliny the Younger and Pliny the Elder, Tacitus, Titus, Trajan (empire largest in 117 CE), Caracalla (decree of 212 CE), Constantine (new capital 330), Alaric (Visigoths entered Rome in 410), Odoacer, Romulus Augustulus (last western emperor, deposed 476 CE), Zeno. Peoples and terms: Gauls, Celtic, Carthaginian, Visigoths, Vandals, Goths, Ottoman Turks, Byzantine, Romans, Greek, Latin, Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Romanian, SPQR (Senate and People of Rome), Consuls, Senate, Plebeians, Tribunes, Magistrates, Veto, Legions, Legion, Auxiliaries, Garrison, Insignia, Pumice, Gladiators, Gladiator, Colosseum, Appian Way, Pax Romana, Ides of March, Punic Wars, Fortress, Tavern, Taverns, Tyrant, Dictator, Republic, Empire, Emperor, Citizenship, Citizens, Stabiae, Juno, Delayer. Voice and tone: lively, clear and fair; legends are told as legends, and the narrator says where historians disagree; dates are traditional or approximate where they are uncertain; deaths and slavery are stated plainly, without gore; no invented quotations.

beats.scene: Seven green hills beside a river where a small city begins
beats.summary: Rome began as a few villages on low hills beside the Tiber, and the Romans told a story about it.

beats.scene: A basket holding two babies drifts down a river past reeds
beats.summary: In the legend, twin boys Romulus and Remus were set adrift on the Tiber.

beats.scene: A she-wolf stands over two babies in a shady cave
beats.summary: A she-wolf fed the twins, and the shepherd Faustulus found and raised them.

beats.scene: Romulus ploughs a line for a new wall while Remus watches
beats.summary: The brothers quarrelled over their new city, and Romulus became its first king, traditionally in 753 BCE.

beats.scene: Archaeologists brush the floor of an ancient hut on a hill
beats.summary: Archaeology shows small villages on the Palatine from about the eighth century BCE, but cannot prove Romulus lived.

beats.scene: Seven stern crowned kings in a row carved on a stone wall
beats.summary: By tradition seven kings ruled Rome; the last, Tarquin the Proud, was hated.

beats.scene: A young noblewoman weeps before her father and husband in a candlelit hall
beats.summary: In the legend, the king's son wronged a noblewoman named Lucretia, and her death outraged Rome.

beats.scene: Brutus holds up a knife before a crowd of angry Romans
beats.summary: Lucius Junius Brutus led the people, and the king was driven out, traditionally in 509 BCE.

beats.scene: Two men in white togas with rods of office sit in a forum
beats.summary: Rome chose two consuls each year, who could each veto the other.

beats.scene: Senators in togas and a crowd of citizens gather below a banner
beats.summary: The state was called the Senate and People of Rome (SPQR), but rich families held most power until the plebeians won tribunes.

beats.scene: A huge army of warriors with long moustaches and shields crosses a river
beats.summary: About 390 BCE a Gaulish war band under Brennus marched south towards Rome.

beats.scene: Panicked Roman soldiers flee across a river beside a hill
beats.summary: The Romans were beaten at the river Allia, a short march from Rome.

beats.scene: Smoke rises from burning houses while a few defenders hold a hilltop
beats.summary: The Gauls entered the empty city and burned much of it, but defenders held the Capitoline Hill.

beats.scene: Geese honk loudly in a temple garden while a soldier wakes
beats.summary: In the legend, sacred geese woke the defenders when the Gauls climbed the hill by night.

beats.scene: A Roman leader holds a sword beside scales weighing gold
beats.summary: The Gauls left after a payment of gold, and Rome was rebuilt with a strong stone wall.

beats.scene: Ships of two navies sail beneath the walls of a rich harbour city
beats.summary: Rome and Carthage fought three Punic Wars, from 264 to 146 BCE.

beats.scene: A long line of elephants and soldiers climbs an icy mountain pass
beats.summary: In 218 BCE Hannibal led an army with elephants across the Alps into Italy.

beats.scene: A huge Roman army faces a smaller army on a flat plain
beats.summary: At Cannae in 216 BCE Hannibal surrounded the Roman army and destroyed it.

beats.scene: Roman senators in dark robes stand in a silent forum after bad news
beats.summary: Rome refused to surrender and raised new armies, while Fabius avoided big battles.

beats.scene: A Roman general stands on a hill above a battlefield in Africa
beats.summary: Scipio attacked Carthage itself and beat Hannibal at Zama in 202 BCE; Carthage was destroyed in 146 BCE.

beats.scene: Gladiators train with wooden swords in a sandy yard
beats.summary: By 73 BCE Rome relied on slave labour, and some slaves were trained as gladiators.

beats.scene: Gladiators with kitchen knives burst out of a school gate in Capua
beats.summary: In 73 BCE Spartacus and about seventy gladiators escaped from a school at Capua.

beats.scene: A growing crowd of men, women and families with wagons climbs a mountain road
beats.summary: Thousands of slaves joined, and the rebels defeated several Roman forces.

beats.scene: A Roman general in a red cloak marches legions across a hillside
beats.summary: Crassus crushed the revolt in 71 BCE, and Spartacus died in the fighting.

beats.scene: A line of grey roadside stones marks the Appian Way at dusk
beats.summary: The revolt did not end slavery, but the name of Spartacus lived on.

beats.scene: A general in a red cloak speaks to soldiers in a Gaulish camp
beats.summary: From 58 to 50 BCE Caesar conquered Gaul and won fame, wealth and loyal soldiers.

beats.scene: Senators in a hall argue while one holds out a letter
beats.summary: Caesar's enemies, backed by Pompey, ordered him to give up his army.

beats.scene: Soldiers stand beside a small river at dawn, a general in front
beats.summary: In January 49 BCE Caesar crossed the Rubicon with one legion, which meant civil war.

beats.scene: Caesar rides into Rome as crowds throw flowers
beats.summary: Caesar won the civil war and became dictator for life in 44 BCE.

beats.scene: Senators surround a man in a toga on the steps of a hall
beats.summary: On 15 March 44 BCE, senators led by Brutus and Cassius killed Caesar.

beats.scene: A teenage boy in a plain toga listens as a will is read aloud
beats.summary: Caesar's will made his great-nephew Octavian, aged eighteen, his heir.

beats.scene: Warships with bronze rams clash at sea near a rocky coast
beats.summary: Octavian beat Antony and Cleopatra at the sea battle of Actium in 31 BCE.

beats.scene: Senators in white togas bow to a calm man in a plain robe
beats.summary: In 27 BCE the Senate gave Octavian the name Augustus, and he became the first emperor.

beats.scene: A busy new road with milestones and a marble temple being built
beats.summary: Augustus ruled until 14 CE and began about two centuries of general peace, the Pax Romana.

beats.scene: Officials and clerks sort scrolls and tax records in a provincial office
beats.summary: The empire was run by governors, tax collectors and soldiers; Latin and Greek were its main languages.

beats.scene: A sunny Roman street with shops, a bakery and a fountain
beats.summary: Pompeii in 79 CE was a busy town on the Bay of Naples under a mountain called Vesuvius.

beats.scene: A tall dark cloud rises from a mountain above a calm bay
beats.summary: Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE, and Pliny the Younger described the cloud from across the bay.

beats.scene: Townspeople carry bundles through falling grey stones and ash
beats.summary: Ash and pumice buried Pompeii; some people fled, others were trapped.

beats.scene: A ship sails towards a shore under a rain of ash
beats.summary: Pliny the Elder sailed to rescue people and died at Stabiae.

beats.scene: A plaster cast of a seated figure lies in a dig in Pompeii
beats.summary: Pompeii lay buried until the eighteenth century, and now shows Roman daily life; Rome itself carried on.

beats.scene: A Roman citizen shows a bronze tablet with his name to a magistrate
beats.summary: Roman citizenship was a valuable privilege that most subjects did not have.

beats.scene: A veteran soldier receives a bronze certificate after many years of service
beats.summary: Non-citizen soldiers usually received citizenship after about twenty-five years of service.

beats.scene: A huge map of the empire stretches from Britain to the Persian Gulf
beats.summary: In 117 CE, under Trajan, the empire reached its greatest size.

beats.scene: A messenger reads a decree aloud before a crowd in a provincial town
beats.summary: In 212 CE Caracalla made almost all free people in the empire citizens.

beats.scene: People of many origins stand together in a crowded provincial market
beats.summary: Slaves were left out, but being Roman now meant legal status, not birth in Italy.

beats.scene: Cracked walls and a worried emperor beside a map of many borders
beats.summary: In the third century the empire suffered crises, and in 330 Constantine founded Constantinople.

beats.scene: Warriors in cloaks cross a frozen river into Roman land
beats.summary: Goths, Vandals and others entered Roman land, and the Visigoths sacked Rome in 410.

beats.scene: A boy in an imperial purple robe is led away from a throne
beats.summary: In 476 CE Odoacer removed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus, the last in the west.

beats.scene: Golden domes of Constantinople rise over a bright blue strait
beats.summary: The Roman Empire in the east lasted until 1453, when the Ottoman Turks took Constantinople.

beats.scene: A Rome street with an ancient arch, a café and a manhole cover
beats.summary: Rome's legacy lives on in languages, law and roads, and SPQR is still on its manhole covers.

B1B2: Rome stands beside the river Tiber, on a group of low hills. Long before it ruled an empire, it was a small place where shepherds and farmers lived in simple huts.
The legend says that twin brothers, Romulus and Remus, were born to a princess and set adrift on the river by a cruel king. Their basket drifted ashore, and the babies were saved.
A she-wolf found the babies and fed them with her milk. Later a shepherd named Faustulus discovered them and raised them as his own sons.

The twins grew up and decided to found a city, but they quarrelled about where it should stand. In the best-known version, Romulus killed his brother and became the first king, and the Romans dated this to 753 BCE.
Archaeologists have found traces of small huts on the Palatine Hill that date from about the eighth century BCE. This fits the legend roughly, but nobody can prove that Romulus ever lived.
By old tradition, seven kings ruled the city of Rome one after another. The last of them, Tarquin the Proud, was feared and disliked because he ruled by force and ignored the Senate.
In the legend, the king's son harmed a noblewoman named Lucretia, and she told her father and husband what he had done. She died soon afterwards, and her death made the Romans furious.
A nobleman named Lucius Junius Brutus called the people together and swore to end the rule of kings. Tarquin was driven out of the city, and this happened, by tradition, in 509 BCE.
After the kings, Rome chose two leaders, called consuls, every year. Each could stop the other from acting, so no single man could hold power for long.

Rome's government was called the Senate and People of Rome, and its initials, SPQR, were carved on buildings and coins. In practice, rich families held most of the power, and ordinary citizens had to fight for their rights.
Around 390 BCE, a large band of Gauls, led by a chieftain named Brennus, marched south into Italy. They were warriors from beyond the Alps who wanted land and treasure.
The two armies met at the river Allia, only a short march north of Rome. The Gauls charged hard, the Roman line broke, and many soldiers ran for their lives.
The Gauls marched into Rome and burned many of its buildings, because most of the people had fled. A small group of defenders held on to the Capitoline Hill, the strongest place in the city.
One night the Gauls crept up the steep hill in the dark. According to the story, the sacred geese of a temple began to honk, and the Romans woke in time to push the attackers back.
After some months, the Gauls left, and the story says that the Romans paid them in gold. Rome was rebuilt, and in the next years its people built a strong new wall around the city.
By about 270 BCE, Rome ruled most of Italy and was growing stronger every year. Across the sea in North Africa, the rich trading city of Carthage was its rival, and the two fought three long wars.
In 218 BCE, the Carthaginian general Hannibal marched an army from Spain over the Alps into Italy. He took elephants with him, and many men and animals died in the cold and snow.
At the battle of Cannae in 216 BCE, Hannibal let the middle of his line fall back. The Romans pushed forward, and his army closed round them like a trap.
After Cannae, many allies left Rome, but the Senate refused to make peace. New armies were raised, and a cautious general named Fabius avoided big battles and wore Hannibal down.
A young general named Scipio took the war to North Africa. In 202 BCE, at the battle of Zama, he defeated Hannibal, and Carthage had to accept Rome's terms.
By about 73 BCE, huge numbers of people in Italy lived as slaves, working on farms, in houses and in mines. Some were trained as gladiators, who fought in public shows for the crowd's entertainment.
Spartacus, a gladiator from Thrace, escaped from a training school in the city of Capua with about seventy others. They broke out using kitchen knives, and then captured better weapons on the road.
Slaves from farms all over southern Italy joined the rebels, and their army grew to tens of thousands. They defeated several Roman forces, and for almost two years they roamed the countryside.
The Senate finally gave command to a very rich man named Crassus, who raised a large army. In 71 BCE, he defeated the rebels in a hard battle, and Spartacus died in the fighting.
The revolt did not end slavery, which remained a part of Roman life for centuries. Even so, the name of Spartacus survived, and people have told his story for more than two thousand years.
From 58 to 50 BCE, Julius Caesar led Roman armies in Gaul, which is now France. He won great victories, grew very famous and rich, and his soldiers were fiercely loyal to him.
Caesar's enemies in the Senate, who were supported by the general Pompey, ordered him to give up his army and come home. He feared that if he obeyed he would be put on trial and lose everything.
In January 49 BCE, Caesar led one legion across the little river Rubicon, the border of his province. Crossing it with an army was against the law, and it meant civil war.
Caesar defeated Pompey and the other leaders of the Senate in a long civil war. By 44 BCE, he had been named dictator for life, which meant that he could not be legally removed.
On the fifteenth of March, 44 BCE, a group of senators attacked Caesar in a meeting hall and killed him. Their leaders were Brutus and Cassius, and they believed they were saving the Republic.
Caesar's will named his great-nephew Octavian, who was only eighteen, as his adopted son. The young man took his great-uncle's name and began to gather his old supporters.
After years of civil war, Octavian faced Mark Antony and Cleopatra, the queen of Egypt, at sea. At the battle of Actium in 31 BCE, his fleet won, and Antony and Cleopatra fled.
In 27 BCE, the Senate gave Octavian a new name, Augustus, which suggests something respected and holy. He said he was only the first citizen of Rome, but in fact he was its first emperor.
Augustus ruled until he died in 14 CE, and he built roads, temples and a fire brigade for the city. His rule began about two hundred years of general peace inside the empire, known as the Pax Romana.
The empire was run by governors, tax collectors and soldiers, who were sent out from Rome. People in the west mostly spoke Latin, while in the east most of them continued to speak Greek.
Pompeii was a lively Roman town near the Bay of Naples, with shops, bars, bakeries and public baths. Its walls were covered with painted notices and with scribbled messages from ordinary people.
In 79 CE, the mountain exploded, and a huge column of ash and smoke rose high into the sky. A young man named Pliny, who watched from across the bay, said that it looked like a pine tree.
For many hours, ash and light stones rained down on Pompeii, and roofs began to collapse. Many people escaped by road or by sea, but others stayed behind and were trapped.
Pliny's uncle, who was a scholar and a commander of the fleet, sailed across the bay to rescue people. He reached the far shore, but he died there, probably from the poisonous air.

Pompeii and nearby Herculaneum stayed buried for about seventeen hundred years, until diggers began to uncover them in the eighteenth century. Today they show us ordinary Roman life with striking clarity.
In the early empire, being a Roman citizen was a valuable privilege. A citizen had legal protections, including the right to a fair trial, and he could not easily be punished without one.
Many soldiers in the Roman army came from conquered lands. If they served for about twenty-five years, they were usually rewarded with citizenship.
Under the emperor Trajan, the empire reached its greatest size in 117 CE, stretching from Britain to the Middle East. It held tens of millions of people, speaking dozens of languages.
In 212 CE, the emperor Caracalla gave Roman citizenship to nearly everyone who was free in the empire. Historians think that he may have wanted more taxes, but the change was enormous.
The new law did not include slaves, and free people did not become equal in wealth or power. Still, Roman identity was now a matter of law, not of birth in Italy.
In the third century, the empire suffered civil wars, plagues and attacks on its borders. Later emperors shared the work of ruling, and in 330 Constantine opened a new capital called Constantinople.
In the fourth and fifth centuries, groups such as the Goths and the Vandals crossed into Roman land. In 410, the Visigoths entered the city of Rome itself, which shocked the whole Roman world.

In 476 CE, a Germanic general named Odoacer removed the last western emperor, a boy named Romulus Augustulus. Odoacer did not take the title, and he sent the imperial symbols to the emperor in Constantinople.
The Roman Empire in the east, centred on Constantinople, lasted for almost another thousand years. It finally ended in 1453, when the Ottoman Turks captured the city.

Latin became Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian, and Roman ideas about law and government still shape the modern world. If you visit the city today, you can see the letters SPQR on the manhole covers.
C1C2: The city of Rome grew beside the river Tiber, on a cluster of low hills that the Romans later counted as seven. Before it ruled an empire, it was a small place of huts and pens, where shepherds and farmers kept animals and watched the river for floods. The Romans themselves, however, preferred to tell a more dramatic story about their beginning.

According to the legend, Romulus and Remus were twin sons of a princess named Rhea Silvia, and a jealous king who feared them ordered the babies to be left to the river. Their basket drifted into shallow water beneath a fig tree and stuck fast in the mud. The Romans told this tale for centuries, though no one now believes that it happened as written.

In the story, a she-wolf found the abandoned babies and fed them with her milk, and a woodpecker is said to have brought them food as well. A shepherd named Faustulus discovered the twins and took them home, and they grew up strong and bold among his flocks. The image of the wolf and the twins has remained the symbol of Rome ever since, and it can still be seen on statues, coins and fountains.

When the twins grew up, they decided to found a city of their own, but they quarrelled bitterly about the place and about who should rule it. In the best-known version of the tale, Romulus killed his brother after Remus mocked the low wall that he had begun to build, and so Romulus became the first king of the city that bears his name. Later Romans calculated that this took place in 753 BCE, and they counted their years from it.

Archaeologists have uncovered the post holes of small round huts on the Palatine Hill, dating from around the eighth century BCE, which fits the legend surprisingly well. Nothing they have found, however, proves that a man named Romulus ever existed, and many historians believe that he was invented to explain the city's name. The story therefore tells us less about the founding than about how the Romans wished to see themselves: as tough, quarrelsome and favoured by the gods.

According to Roman tradition, seven kings ruled the city in turn, some wise and some warlike, over a period of about two hundred and fifty years. The last of them, Tarquin the Proud, was remembered as a tyrant who ignored the advice of the Senate, punished his enemies and treated the nobles as servants. Modern historians think that the details are legend, but a long period of royal rule probably did come before the republic.

The legend says that the king's son wronged a noblewoman named Lucretia, who told her father and her husband what had happened and then took her own life rather than live with the shame. Her death, in the story, turned grief into rage, and the whole city began to feel that no family was safe from the king. Historians cannot tell whether she was real, but the tale shows how the Romans understood freedom: as protection from the whims of one man.

A nobleman named Lucius Junius Brutus, who was said to be a relative of Lucretia, called the citizens together and made them swear never again to accept a king. While Tarquin was away with the army, the gates of Rome were closed against him, and he never returned to rule the city. The Romans placed this revolution in 509 BCE, and the very word king remained hateful to them for the rest of their history.

In place of a king, the Romans elected two magistrates called consuls, who served for just one year and who each held the power to veto the other. The idea was to prevent any individual from gathering too much strength, and it was reinforced by a strong dislike of anyone who seemed to desire a crown. This system, with many changes and many exceptions, lasted for nearly five hundred years.

The Romans spoke of their state as the Senate and People of Rome, and the four letters SPQR, which stand for those words, were carved on buildings and stitched on army banners. In reality, wealthy families filled the Senate and controlled most offices, and ordinary citizens, known as plebeians, had to struggle for a voice. According to tradition, they went on strike in 494 BCE and won the right to elect their own officials, called tribunes, who could protect them from unfair treatment.

Around 390 BCE, a large war band of Gauls, led according to the Roman historians by a chieftain called Brennus, swept south through northern Italy towards Rome. These were Celtic-speaking warriors from beyond the Alps, famous for their long swords, their loud war cries and their willingness to charge at almost any enemy. At that time Rome was an ambitious city, but it was still only one of many in Italy and had no real experience of an enemy like this.

The two armies met beside the river Allia, about eighteen kilometres from Rome, and the battle was over almost before it began. The Roman line, which had been stretched too thin, broke under the first fierce charge, and many soldiers fled in panic, reportedly throwing away their shields as they ran. The anniversary of the defeat was remembered afterwards as an unlucky day in the Roman calendar.

Most of the population had fled before the Gauls arrived, and the invaders marched into a half-empty city, plundering houses and setting fire to many of them. A small garrison, however, held the Capitoline Hill, the strongest fortress in Rome, where the defenders watched the smoke rise and wondered how long their food would last. Archaeologists have found some traces of burning from about this time, although they cannot always tell which fires the Gauls set.

According to the story, the Gauls tried to climb the hill by night, creeping quietly past the sleeping guards and even the guard dogs. But the geese kept in the temple of Juno, which the starving defenders had somehow not eaten, began to honk and flap, and a soldier named Marcus Manlius woke and hurled the first climber back down the slope. The Romans honoured geese for it long afterwards, which may be some small comfort to any goose that has ever been served for dinner.

After several months of siege, the Gauls accepted a payment of gold and went away, though one legend claims that a Roman general, Camillus, arrived at the last moment and drove them out instead. Rome was rebuilt in haste, and a few years later its people raised a great stone wall nearly eleven kilometres long. The lesson that the Romans drew from this disaster was never to be caught unprepared again, and it may have helped to make them so determined in later wars.

By about 270 BCE, Rome had won control of most of Italy, and its attention turned to the sea. Facing it across the water was Carthage, a wealthy trading city in North Africa whose fleets and silver mines made it the greatest power in the western Mediterranean. Between 264 and 146 BCE the two states fought three wars, known as the Punic Wars, and the contest decided which of them would rule the region.

In 218 BCE, during the second war, the Carthaginian general Hannibal led an army from Spain across southern Gaul and over the Alps, hoping to strike at Rome in its own country. He brought war elephants with him, and the crossing in snow and ice cost him thousands of men, together with most of his animals. Yet he arrived in Italy with a force that was smaller, but also tougher and more experienced than before.

At Cannae, in southern Italy, in the summer of 216 BCE, the Romans sent a much larger army against Hannibal, confident that numbers would win. He deliberately let the centre of his line give way, so that the Romans pressed forward into a pocket while his best troops closed in on both sides. Tens of thousands of Roman soldiers died in a single afternoon, and the battle is still studied in military schools as a masterpiece of tactics.

Many of Rome's allies in southern Italy deserted after Cannae, and Hannibal expected the Senate to ask for terms, but no such request came. Instead, Rome raised new legions from boys and even from slaves who volunteered, and it avoided open battle with Hannibal, following the cautious plan of Fabius, whom people nicknamed the Delayer. The decision never to surrender, even after the worst defeat in its history, became a central part of the Roman character.

A young general named Scipio decided that the way to remove Hannibal from Italy was to attack Carthage itself, and he landed an army in North Africa. At the battle of Zama in 202 BCE, he defeated Hannibal at last, and Carthage was forced to accept harsh peace terms. Half a century later, in 146 BCE, Rome destroyed the city completely at the end of the third war, and the Mediterranean was left without a rival to its power.

By about 73 BCE, Rome's conquests had brought huge numbers of captives to Italy, and slaves worked on farms, in mines, in workshops and in the houses of the rich. Some of them were trained in special schools as gladiators, who were forced to fight in public shows while crowds cheered or booed. Their lives belonged entirely to their owners, and the Romans, who prided themselves on their order, rarely looked closely at this fact.

Spartacus, a gladiator from Thrace, in the Balkans, led a breakout from a training school at Capua with about seventy companions, armed only with kitchen knives and spits. On the road they captured a wagon of real weapons, defeated the soldiers sent after them, and took refuge on the slopes of Mount Vesuvius. The Roman authorities, who had considered the escape a minor police matter, soon discovered how wrong they were.

Slaves from farms and ranches all over southern Italy joined him, and the army grew into tens of thousands of men, women and children, though ancient writers disagree about the exact number. It defeated several Roman forces in turn, and for almost two years the rebels roamed across southern Italy, plundering estates and freeing others as they went. The Senate, which had never expected to be threatened by slaves, was thoroughly alarmed.

At last the Senate gave command to a very wealthy politician called Marcus Licinius Crassus, who raised a large army and drove the rebels into the south of Italy. In 71 BCE, he defeated them in a final bloody battle, in which Spartacus is believed to have died, though his body was never identified. Roman soldiers later put about six thousand captured rebels to death along the road called the Appian Way, as a warning to others.

The rising did not end slavery, which remained a basic part of Roman life for many centuries, and few Romans seriously questioned the system itself. Yet the name of Spartacus, who had once been a nobody, lasted longer than those of most senators of his day, and his story has been retold in books, plays and films ever since. It is a reminder that the glories of Rome were built on a society in which millions of people had no freedom at all.

Between 58 and 50 BCE, the ambitious politician Julius Caesar led Roman armies through Gaul, which covered most of modern France, and brought the whole country under Roman rule. His victories made him famous and enormously rich, and his soldiers, who shared in the glory and the loot, were fiercely loyal to him personally. In the Roman Republic, such a combination of fame, wealth and loyal legions was both a great asset and a great danger.

Caesar's enemies in the Senate, supported by the famous general Pompey, who had once been his ally, ordered him to give up his army and return to Rome as an ordinary citizen. Caesar believed that, without his legions to protect him, he would be put on trial by his rivals and ruined. He therefore faced a choice between obedience and civil war, and he weighed it carefully.

In January of 49 BCE, Caesar led a single legion across the Rubicon, a small river that marked the border between his province and Italy itself. It was a crime for a general to bring an army over that line, and he is said to have declared, as he crossed, that the die was cast. The phrase crossing the Rubicon has meant taking a step that cannot be reversed ever since.

Pompey fled when Caesar advanced, but the fighting spread across the Mediterranean and lasted for four years, and Caesar was victorious in the end. He reformed the calendar, planned new buildings and gave land to his veterans, and early in 44 BCE he accepted the title of dictator for life. Many senators, who had spent their lives defending the Republic, felt that they had lost their freedom in all but name.

On the Ides of March, which was the fifteenth, in 44 BCE, dozens of senators surrounded Caesar at a meeting and stabbed him to death. Their leaders, Marcus Brutus and Gaius Cassius, believed that they were rescuing the Republic from a tyrant, and they expected the people to cheer. Instead, Rome fell into more than a decade of civil war, and the Republic they had hoped to save was gone for good.

In his will, Caesar had adopted his young great-nephew Octavian, who was then only eighteen and studying far from Rome, and had made him his heir. Octavian, a thin and often unwell young man whom nobody took seriously, hurried to Rome, took the name Caesar, and rallied the dead man's veterans to his side. Within a few years, the boy whom the politicians had despised was one of the most powerful men in the Roman world.

After years of civil war, only two rivals remained: Octavian, and Mark Antony, who had joined forces with Cleopatra, the queen of Egypt. In 31 BCE their fleets met at Actium, off the western coast of Greece, and Octavian's admiral Agrippa won a decisive victory. Antony and Cleopatra fled to Egypt, and within a year both were dead, and Octavian ruled the entire Mediterranean world.

In 27 BCE, the Senate granted Octavian the title Augustus, a word that suggested something more than human, and he became the first emperor of Rome. He was careful, however, to keep the old institutions in place and to call himself merely the first citizen, so that the senators could pretend that the Republic still lived. It was a clever disguise, and it allowed one man to rule an empire without ever calling himself a king.

Augustus ruled for more than forty years and died in 14 CE, having rebuilt much of the capital, organised a fire brigade and a police force, and repaired the roads of Italy. He boasted that he had found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble, and there was some truth in the claim. His rule began roughly two centuries of general peace within the empire, called the Pax Romana, although there was still fighting on the frontiers.

To run so vast a territory, the emperors depended on governors, tax collectors, army officers and a growing civil service, all connected by the road system and by letters that travelled for weeks. Latin became the language of law and the army in the western provinces, while in the east educated people continued to speak and write Greek. Despite its size, the empire's local life stayed varied, for the Romans seldom cared what gods or customs their subjects kept so long as they paid their taxes.

In the year 79 CE, Pompeii was a prosperous town of perhaps eleven thousand people on the Bay of Naples, with bakeries, taverns, theatres, public baths and a busy market. Its walls carried election slogans, advertisements and scribbled jokes, which give us a rare chance to hear ordinary Romans, not just emperors and senators. Nearby stood the mountain Vesuvius, green with vineyards, and few of the townspeople realised that it was a volcano.

One day in 79 CE the mountain erupted, throwing a column of ash, smoke and stone many kilometres into the sky. A teenager named Pliny, who watched from across the bay, later wrote that the cloud looked like an umbrella pine, with a tall trunk and spreading branches at the top. His letters, written years afterwards to the historian Tacitus, are one of the few eyewitness accounts of a volcanic eruption from the ancient world.

For many hours, ash and small, light stones called pumice fell on Pompeii until the streets were deep in grey, and roofs began to give way under the weight. Many of the townspeople escaped by road or boat, carrying what they could, but some stayed behind, hoping the danger would pass, or could not leave. In the early hours of the next morning, rushing clouds of hot gas and ash swept through the town, and no one still in the streets or houses survived.

The elder Pliny, a famous scholar who commanded the Roman fleet at Misenum, ordered ships to cross the bay to rescue people stranded on the shore, and he sailed with them to see the event for himself. He reached the town of Stabiae, where the wind blocked his return, and he died there on the beach, probably from the choking air. His nephew's account gives us a rare glimpse of a man who put curiosity and duty before his own safety.

The buried towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum slept under ash for about seventeen hundred years, until excavations began in the eighteenth century. The deep layer of ash preserved bread, paintings, furniture and even graffiti, and the hollows left by the bodies of victims have been filled with plaster to show their final poses. Meanwhile, in Rome itself, life went on, and in 80 CE the emperor Titus opened the Colosseum, an enormous arena that held tens of thousands of spectators.

Roman citizenship was a precious privilege, and during the first two centuries of the empire most people who lived under Roman rule did not have it. A citizen enjoyed legal protections, including the right to appeal against certain punishments and to be tried in a proper court, and he could travel the empire with a certain confidence. Citizenship was a reward, to be earned by service in the army or granted to loyal communities and individuals.

Many of the soldiers in the Roman army were not citizens at all but came from conquered lands, and they served in special units called auxiliaries. After about twenty-five years, a veteran was usually rewarded with citizenship, which was recorded on a bronze certificate that he could carry home. In this way, the army became one of the great machines for turning subjects into Romans, whether they came from Spain, Syria or the banks of the Danube.

In 117 CE, under the emperor Trajan, the Roman Empire reached its greatest extent, stretching from Britain to the deserts of Egypt and east towards the Persian Gulf. It held tens of millions of people, who spoke dozens of languages and worshipped hundreds of gods, and their only common bond was Roman rule. It was an enormous territory to govern, and the question of who really belonged to Rome grew harder to answer with every new province.

In 212 CE, the emperor Caracalla issued a decree that made almost every free person in the empire a Roman citizen, from a farmer in Egypt to a merchant in Gaul. Some historians suspect that his motive was money, since citizens paid certain taxes, but whatever his reason, the effect was remarkable. A privilege that had once belonged to a small group of Italians was now shared by many millions of people.

The decree did not include slaves, and it did not make rich and poor equal, since powerful families still held most of the wealth and the best positions. Even so, it meant that being Roman was now a matter of law, not of birth in the city of Rome or in Italy. Many emperors came from the provinces, from Spain, Syria and Africa, a fact that would have astonished the senators of the old Republic.

During the third century CE, the empire was shaken by civil wars, outbreaks of disease and attacks along its frontiers, and some emperors held power for only a few months. Later rulers divided the work of governing between east and west, and in 330 Constantine dedicated a new capital on the Bosporus, which was named Constantinople. The wealthier eastern half proved the stronger, while the west grew poorer and harder to defend.

In the fourth and fifth centuries, peoples from beyond the frontier, among them the Goths and the Vandals, moved into Roman territory, sometimes as invited allies and sometimes as invaders. In 410 the Visigoths, led by Alaric, entered the city of Rome and plundered it for three days, a shock that echoed throughout the Roman world. Historians still debate how much of the decline was caused by outside pressure and how much by weakness within.

In 476 CE, a general of Germanic origin named Odoacer removed the last emperor of the west, a teenager with the remarkable name Romulus Augustulus, which echoed that of the city's legendary founder. Odoacer spared the boy, sent him to live comfortably in southern Italy, and returned the imperial insignia to the emperor in Constantinople, as though the west no longer needed an emperor of its own. Later historians treated that quiet moment as the end of the Roman Empire in the West, though few people at the time would have seen it as a dramatic turning point.

In the east, the Roman Empire went on, with its capital at Constantinople, and its people still called themselves Romans although they spoke Greek. Modern historians call it the Byzantine Empire, and it survived for almost a thousand years after the end of the west, until the Ottoman Turks captured its capital in 1453. For long stretches of that time, the successors of Augustus ruled a state that was richer and more sophisticated than most of the kingdoms of Europe.

The Roman Empire left a long shadow: Latin turned slowly into Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian, and Roman law became the foundation of many modern legal systems. Even the question that preoccupied the Romans, whether a republic can stay free once its power grows great, has not gone away. In the streets of Rome today, the four letters SPQR are still stamped on the manhole covers, as though the Senate and People were quietly keeping an eye on the city.
